diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $c=c(M,T)$ be the maximum of $1$ and the implicit constants from \eqref{eq:Rekalpha4H1} and \eqref{eq:Rekalpha4L2}.

issues.failure_explanation: In the induction that closes the recursion Err_m <= 2c(Err_{m-1} + tau^{1/2}) for alpha=4, the term c*T_1^{1/2}*Err_m must be absorbed, which requires c*T_1^{1/2} <= 1/2. But with c defined only as the maximum of 1 and the implicit constants of the recursions and with T_1 <= c^{-2}, one can only conclude c*T_1^{1/2} <= 1. Hence the displayed inference 'c T_1^{1/2} Err_m <= (1/2) Err_m' is unjustified as written, and the induction/recursion on which both error bounds of the alpha=4 case rely does not close.

failure_location.quote: \mathrm{Err}_m \le c\|E_{N_m}\|_{H^1 \times L^2} + c\tau^\frac12 + cT_1^{\frac12}\mathrm{Err}_m \le c\mathrm{Err}_{m-1} + c\tau^\frac12 + \frac12 \mathrm{Err}_m

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Shrink the constant in the definition of T_1 (e.g. T_1 := min{T, b_0, (2c)^{-2}}, or alternatively define c as twice the maximum of 1 and the implicit constants), so that c*T_1^{1/2} <= 1/2; the absorption step, the recursion Err_m <= 2c(Err_{m-1}+tau^{1/2}), and all subsequent definitions (L, C, tau_0) then go through unchanged.
issues.overall_effect: The H^1 x L^2 and L^2 x H^{-1} error bounds of Theorem ThmStrang for alpha=4 lack a complete proof as stated; since the proof of Theorem ThmStrangFully is finished 'as in the semi-discrete case above', its alpha=4 bound inherits the same gap.
issues.title: Absorption step in the alpha=4 energy iteration for Theorem ThmStrang fails with the stated choice of T_1
issues.why_classification: A single local constant repair (redefining T_1 or c) closes the induction; the method, both convergence rates, and the advertised scope all survive with no new argument.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Here it is important to use the interpolation error estimate from Lemma \ref{LemTrigIntStab} with $q = 6/5$. If we stuck to $L^2$-based estimates, we could for the $L^2 \times H^{-1}$ norm only reach a sub-optimal estimate of order $K^{-1/2}$

issues.failure_explanation: The W^{1,6/5} norm of g(pi_N u) contains the term ||g(pi_N u)||_{L^{6/5}}, which is not controlled by the derivative term ||g'(pi_N u)||_{L^3}||pi_N grad u||_{L^2} used in the next step (for a spatially constant solution u the latter vanishes while the former is nonzero). Retaining the dropped term gives only K^{-1} N^{1/2} <= K^{-1/2}. Thus the claimed optimal bound ||P~_n||_{L^2 x H^{-1}} <= C K^{-1} does not follow from the stated chain of inequalities; only the sub-optimal K^{-1/2} follows from it. (The parallel energy-norm chain drops the same term, but there its K^{-1/2} conclusion survives via Bernstein.)
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the faulty step by a decomposition: g(pi_{K/alpha}u) has frequencies <= K and is therefore exactly reproduced by the (2K+1)^3-point interpolant, so (I-I_K)g(pi_N u) = (I-I_K)[g(pi_N u) - g(pi_{K/alpha}u)]; bound this remainder via the Lipschitz estimate for g, Hoelder, Lemma LemPiNew for (I-pi_{K/alpha})u, the L^q boundedness of I_K on pi_{alpha K}-localized functions (Lemma LemTrigIntStab), and the discrete Strichartz bound for ||pi_N u||_{l^3_tau L^{18}} from Proposition PropStrichUNew, which yields <= C K^{-1} and restores the stated rate.
issues.overall_effect: The spatial order K^{-1} in the L^2 x H^{-1} error bound of Theorem ThmStrangFully for alpha=4 (and analogously for alpha=3), which the paper advertises as optimal in view of the projection error, is not established by the given argument.
issues.title: Fully discrete proof bounds the interpolation-error term P~_n by dropping the L^q part of the W^{1,q} norm, leaving the optimal K^{-1} rate in L^2 x H^{-1} unsupported
issues.why_classification: The invalid inference is central to the advertised optimal spatial rate K^{-1}; restoring it requires a replacement argument (though short and built from the paper's own tools) rather than a constant fix, but no global proof architecture has to change and no stated guarantee is lost.
